text:
Company Overview
We were incorporated in Delaware in 1919 and reincorporated in North Carolina in 1986. We are a leading global beverage and
convenient food company with a comp lementary portfolio of brands, including Lay’s, Doritos, Cheetos, Gatorade, Pepsi-Cola,
Mountain Dew, Quaker and SodaStream . Through our operations, authorized bottlers, contract manufacturers and other third
parties, we make, market, distribute and sell a wide variety of beverages and convenient foods, serving customers and consumers
in more than 200 countries and territories.

title: Our Operations - Introduction
heading: Our Operations
start_phrase: We are or ganized into seven reportable segments (also referred to as divisions), as follows:
summary: This section introduces the company’s organizational structure of seven reportable segments (divisions) and their scopes: Frito-Lay North America (FLNA) for branded convenient foods in the U.S. and Canada; Quaker Foods North America (QFNA) for branded convenient foods including cereal, rice, pasta and other foods in the U.S. and Canada; PepsiCo Beverages North America (PBNA) for beverages in the U.S. and Canada; Latin America (LatAm) for all beverage and convenient food businesses in Latin America; Europe for all beverage and convenient food businesses in Europe; Africa, Middle East and South Asia (AMESA) for all beverage and convenient food businesses across those regions; and Asia Pacific, Australia and New Zealand and China Region (APAC) for all beverage and convenient food businesses across Asia Pacific, Australia and New Zealand, and the China region.

title: Frito-Lay North America
heading: Frito-Lay North America
start_phrase: Either independentl y or in conjunction with third parties, FLNA makes, markets, distributes and sells branded convenient foods.
summary:
- Defines two international segments: AMESA (Africa, Middle East and South Asia) and APAC (Asia Pacific, Australia and New Zealand, and China region), covering both beverage and convenient foods.
- Describes Frito-Lay North America (FLNA): manufactures and sells branded convenient foods (e.g., Cheetos, Doritos, Fritos, Lay’s, Ruffles, Tostitos) primarily through independent distributors and retailers; includes the Sabra refrigerated dips JV with Strauss Group.
- Describes Quaker Foods North America (QFNA): produces cereals, rice, pasta, and other branded foods (e.g., Cap’n Crunch, Life, Pearl Milling Company, Quaker oatmeal/grits/chewy bars/rice cakes/Simply Granola, Rice-A-Roni) sold via independent distributors and retailers.
- Describes PepsiCo Beverages North America (PBNA): makes and sells concentrates, fountain syrups, and finished beverages (e.g., Aquafina, Pepsi, Diet Pepsi, Mountain Dew/Diet, Gatorade/Zero, Propel); operates bottling plants and distribution; sells through independent distributors/retailers and authorized/independent bottlers.
- Highlights PBNA partnerships and licenses: RTD tea/coffee JVs with Unilever (Lipton) and Starbucks; licenses from Keurig Dr Pepper (Crush, Dr Pepper, Schweppes) and juice brands from Dole and Ocean Spray.
- Notes 2022 initiatives: began distributing Hard MTN Dew (manufactured/owned by Boston Beer Company); executed the “Juice Transaction” selling Tropicana, Naked and select juice brands to PAI Partners, forming Tropicana Brands Group (TBG) with a 39% noncontrolling interest; PepsiCo is exclusive U.S. distributor for TBG brands in small-format and foodservice via chilled DSD.
- Describes Latin America (LatAm): produces and sells convenient foods (e.g., Cheetos, Doritos, Emperador, Lay’s, Marias Gamesa, Ruffles, Sabritas, Saladitas, Tostitos, Quaker-branded) and beverages (e.g., 7UP/Diet, Gatorade, H2oh!, Manzanita Sol, Mirinda, Pepsi/Pepsi Black, San Carlos, Toddy) through authorized/independent bottlers, distributors, and retailers.
text:
Frito-Lay North America
Either independentl y or in conjunction with third parties, FLNA makes, markets, distributes and sells branded convenient
foods. These foods include branded dips, Cheetos cheese-flavored snacks, Doritos tortilla chips, Fritos corn chips, Lay’s potato
chips, Ruffles potato  chips and Tostitos tortilla chips. FLNA ’s branded products are sold to independent distributors and retailers.
In addition, FLNA ’s joint venture with Strauss Group makes, markets, distributes and sells Sabra refrigerated dips and spreads.

title: Quaker Foods North America
heading: Quaker Foods North America
start_phrase: Either independently or in conjunction with third parties, QFNA makes, markets, distributes and sells branded convenient foods, which include cereals, rice, pasta and other branded products.
summary:
- Defines two international segments: AMESA (Africa, Middle East and South Asia) and APAC (Asia Pacific, Australia and New Zealand, and China region), covering both beverages and convenient foods in those geographies.
- Describes Frito-Lay North America (FLNA): manufactures and sells branded convenient foods (e.g., Cheetos, Doritos, Fritos, Lay’s, Ruffles, Tostitos, branded dips), sold to independent distributors and retailers; includes a joint venture with Strauss Group for Sabra refrigerated dips and spreads.
- Describes Quaker Foods North America (QFNA): produces cereals and other convenient foods (e.g., Cap’n Crunch, Life, Pearl Milling Company, Quaker oatmeal/grits/rice cakes/Chewy/Simply Granola, Rice-A-Roni), sold to independent distributors and retailers.
- Details PepsiCo Beverages North America (PBNA): makes and sells beverage concentrates, fountain syrups, and finished goods (e.g., Aquafina, Pepsi, Diet Pepsi, Mountain Dew, Diet Mountain Dew, Gatorade, Gatorade Zero, Propel); operates bottling and distribution, sells directly and via authorized/independent bottlers; joint ventures for ready-to-drink tea (Unilever/Lipton) and coffee (Starbucks); licenses certain brands from Keurig Dr Pepper (Crush, Dr Pepper, Schweppes) and juice brands from Dole and Ocean Spray; began distributing Hard MTN Dew (Boston Beer) in 2022; executed the 2022 Juice Transaction selling Tropicana, Naked and other select juice brands to PAI Partners, retaining a 39% noncontrolling interest in Tropicana Brands Group and serving as exclusive U.S. distributor to small-format and foodservice customers via chilled DSD.
- Outlines Latin America (LatAm): produces and sells convenient foods (e.g., Cheetos, Doritos, Emperador, Lay’s, Marias Gamesa, Ruffles, Sabritas, Saladitas, Tostitos, Quaker-branded foods) and beverages (e.g., 7UP, Diet 7UP, Gatorade, H2oh!, Manzanita Sol, Mirinda, Pepsi, Pepsi Black, San Carlos, Toddy), distributed through authorized/independent bottlers, independent distributors, and retailers.
text:
Quaker Foods North America
Either independently or in conjunction with third parties, QFNA makes, markets, distributes and sells branded convenient foods,
which include cereals, rice, pasta and other branded products. QFNA ’s products include Cap’n Crunch cereal, Life cereal, Pearl
Milling Company syrups and mixes, Quaker Chewy granola bars, Quaker grits, Quaker oatmeal, Quaker rice cakes, Quaker
Simply Granola and Rice-A-Roni side dishes. QFNA ’s branded products are sold to independent distributors and retailers.

title: PepsiCo Beverages North America
heading: PepsiCo Beverages North America
start_phrase: Either independently or in conjunction with third parties, PBNA makes, markets and sells beverage concentrates, fountain syrups and finished goods under various beverage brands including Aquafina, Diet Mountain Dew, Diet Pepsi, Gatorade, Gatorade Zero, Mountain Dew, Pepsi and Propel.
summary:
Overview of PepsiCo’s segment structure and activities:
- Defines AMESA (Africa, Middle East and South Asia) and APAC (Asia Pacific, Australia and New Zealand, and China Region) segments.
- Details Frito-Lay North America (FLNA) operations: manufacturing, marketing, distribution and sales of snack brands (Cheetos, Doritos, Fritos, Lay’s, Ruffles, Tostitos, branded dips) primarily through independent distributors and retailers; includes Sabra refrigerated dips JV with Strauss Group.
- Details Quaker Foods North America (QFNA): cereals and convenient foods (Cap’n Crunch, Life, Pearl Milling Company, Quaker oatmeal/grits/granola bars/rice cakes/Simply Granola, Rice-A-Roni) sold via independent distributors and retailers.
- Details PepsiCo Beverages North America (PBNA): concentrates, fountain syrups and finished beverages (Aquafina, Pepsi, Diet Pepsi, Mountain Dew/Diet, Gatorade/Gatorade Zero, Propel); owns bottling and distribution; sells to independent distributors/retailers and to authorized/independent bottlers. Includes RTD tea/coffee JVs with Unilever (Lipton) and Starbucks; licenses brands from Keurig Dr Pepper (Crush, Dr Pepper, Schweppes), and juice brands from Dole and Ocean Spray. Began distributing Hard MTN Dew (Boston Beer Company) in 2022. Completed 2022 sale of Tropicana, Naked and select juice brands to PAI Partners, retaining 39% in Tropicana Brands Group (TBG) operating in North America and Europe; PepsiCo is exclusive U.S. distributor to small-format and foodservice customers via chilled DSD.
- Details Latin America (LatAm): snack brands (Cheetos, Doritos, Emperador, Lay’s, Marias Gamesa, Ruffles, Sabritas, Saladitas, Tostitos, Quaker foods) and beverage brands (7UP/Diet 7UP, Gatorade, H2oh!, Manzanita Sol, Mirinda, Pepsi/Pepsi Black, San Carlos, Toddy) sold through authorized/independent bottlers, independent distributors and retailers.
- Emphasizes multi-channel distribution models across segments, including direct-store-delivery (DSD), independent distributors, retailers and bottler networks.
text:
PepsiCo Beverages North America
Either independently or in conjunction with third parties, PBNA makes, markets and sells beverage concentrates, fountain syrups
and finished goods under various beverage brands including Aquafina, Diet Mountain Dew, Diet Pepsi, Gatorade, Gatorade Zero,
Mountain Dew, Pepsi and Propel. PBN A operates its own bottling plants and distribution facilities and sells branded finished
goods directly to independent distribut ors and retailers. PBNA also sells concentrate and finished goods for our brands to
authorized and independent bottlers, who in turn sell our branded finished goods to independent distributors and retailers in
certain markets. PBNA also, either indep endently or in conjunction with third parties, makes, markets, distributes and sells ready-
to-drink tea and coffee products through joint ventures with Unilever (under the Lipton brand name) and Starbucks, respectively .
Further , PBNA manufactures and distributes certain brands licensed from Keuri g Dr Pepper Inc., including Crush, Dr Pepper and
Schweppes, and certain juice brands licensed from Dole Food Company , Inc. and Ocean Spray Cranberries, Inc. In 2022, PBNA
began to distribute Hard MTN Dew, an alcoholic beverage manufactured and owned by the Boston Beer Company . In the first
quarter of 2022, we sold our Tropicana, Naked and other select juice brands to PAI Partners, while retaining a 39%
noncontrolling interest in a newly formed joint venture, Tropicana Brands Group (TBG), operating across North America and
Europe (Juice Transaction). In the United States, PepsiCo acts as the exclusive distributor for TBG’ s portfolio of brands for
small-format and foodservice customer s with chilled direct-store-delivery (DSD). See Note 13 to our consolidated financial
statements for further information.

summary:
- Overview of PepsiCo’s global operating segments and their scope: FLNA, QFNA, PBNA, Latin America, Europe, Africa/Middle East/South Asia (AMESA), and Asia Pacific/Australia & New Zealand/China (APAC).
- FLNA: U.S. snack portfolio (Lay’s, Doritos, Cheetos, Ruffles, Fritos, Tostitos, branded dips); joint venture with Strauss Group for Sabra refrigerated dips and spreads; sales to independent distributors and retailers.
- QFNA: Branded convenient foods (Quaker oatmeal, grits, rice cakes, Simply Granola; Cap’n Crunch, Life; Pearl Milling Company syrups and mixes; Quaker Chewy; Rice-A-Roni); sales to independent distributors and retailers.
- PBNA: Beverage concentrates, fountain syrups, and finished goods (Pepsi, Diet Pepsi, Mountain Dew, Diet Mountain Dew, Aquafina, Gatorade, Gatorade Zero, Propel); own bottling and distribution plus sales to authorized/independent bottlers; RTD tea and coffee via JVs with Unilever (Lipton) and Starbucks; licenses for Crush, Dr Pepper, Schweppes (from Keurig Dr Pepper) and certain Dole/Ocean Spray juice brands; began distributing Hard MTN Dew (Boston Beer) in 2022; 2022 sale of Tropicana, Naked and select juice brands to PAI Partners with a retained 39% stake in Tropicana Brands Group (TBG) and U.S. chilled DSD exclusivity for small-format and foodservice.
- Latin America: Snack brands (Cheetos, Doritos, Emperador, Lay’s, Marias Gamesa, Ruffles, Sabritas, Saladitas, Tostitos) and Quaker foods; beverages (7UP, Diet 7UP, Gatorade, H2oh!, Manzanita Sol, Mirinda, Pepsi, Pepsi Black, San Carlos, Toddy); sales via authorized/independent bottlers, distributors, and retailers; RTD tea JV with Unilever (Lipton).
- Europe: Snacks (Lay’s, Walkers, Doritos, Cheetos, Ruffles) and Quaker foods via consolidated and noncontrolled affiliates; beverages (7UP, Diet Pepsi, Mirinda, Pepsi, Pepsi Max, Lubimy Sad) with a mix of own bottling and third-party bottlers; SodaStream makers and related products; dairy brands (Agusha, Chudo, Domik v Derevne); RTD tea JV with Unilever; 2022 TBG juice transaction noted.
- AMESA: Snacks (Chipsy, Doritos, Kurkure, Lay’s, Sasko, Spekko, White Star) and Quaker foods via consolidated and noncontrolled affiliates; beverages (7UP, Aquafina, Mirinda, Mountain Dew, Pepsi); mix of own bottling and third-party networks; RTD tea JV with Unilever.
- APAC: Snacks (BaiCaoWei, Cheetos, Doritos, Lay’s, Smith’s) and Quaker foods via consolidated and noncontrolled affiliates; beverages (7UP, Aquafina, Mirinda, Mountain Dew, Pepsi, Sting); RTD tea JV with Unilever.
- Distribution: Multi-channel model using direct-store-delivery (DSD), customer warehouse, distributor networks, and e-commerce; route-to-market tailored by customer needs, product characteristics, and local trade practices.

title: Direct-Store-Delivery
heading: Direct-Store-Delivery
start_phrase: We, our independen t bottlers and our distributors operate DSD systems that deliver beverages and convenient foods directly to retail stores where the products are merchandised by our employees or our independent bottlers.
summary:
- Outlines four go-to-market channels:
  - Direct-Store-Delivery (DSD) for high-turnover products benefiting from frequent restocking, in-store promotion, and merchandising control.
  - Customer warehouse deliveries from company or third-party facilities for less fragile, less perishable, lower-turnover items at lower cost.
  - Third-party distributor networks to expand reach, notably for foodservice and vending channels serving restaurants, businesses, schools, and stadiums.
  - E-commerce sales direct to consumers via company-owned and third-party websites and mobile apps.
- Details key ingredients and inputs used in beverages and convenient foods, including sweeteners (aspartame, sucralose, sugar, corn sweeteners), grains (corn, oats, rice, wheat, flour), potatoes, raw milk, juice concentrates, flavorings, seasonings, vegetable and essential oils, and water.
- Lists major packaging materials and energy needs: PET and polypropylene resins, film packaging, aluminum, glass, closures, cardboard/paperboard, plus fuel, electricity, and natural gas.
- Describes supply assurance and cost management:
  - Use of specialists and diversified sourcing across geographies and suppliers; no significant continuous shortages experienced.
  - Purchasing largely in open markets with exposure to price fluctuations managed via fixed-price contracts, purchase orders, pricing agreements, and derivatives (swaps, futures).
  - Decisions on passing cost increases to customers vary by circumstance.
- Highlights sustainability efforts: integrating recyclability into product development, increasing recycled content (including recycled PET), and advancing sustainable farming practices globally across the agricultural supply chain.
- Notes recent operating headwinds: higher commodity, packaging, and input costs, and supply constraints linked to the Ukraine conflict, COVID-19, inflation, adverse weather, supply chain disruptions, and labor shortages, continuing into fiscal 2023.
- Mentions voluntary supply chain finance programs with global financial institutions, allowing suppliers to sell receivables related to the company.
text:
Direct-Store-Delivery
We, our independen t bottlers and our distributors operate DSD systems that deliver beverages and convenient foods directly to
retail stores where the products are merchandised by our employees or our independent bottlers. DSD enables us to merchandise
with maximum visibility and appeal. DSD is especially well-suited to products that are restocked often and respond to in-store
promotion and merchandising.

Distributor Networks
We distrib ute many  of our products through third-party distributors. Third-p arty distributors are particularly effective when
greater distribution reach can be achiev ed by including a wide range of products on the delivery vehicles. For example, our
foodservice and vending business distributes beverages and convenient foods to restaurants, businesses, schools and stadiums
through third-party foodservice and vending distributors and operators.

text:
Ingredients and Other Supplies
The principal ingredients we use in our beverage and convenient food products are aspartame, corn, corn sweeteners, flavorings,
flour , juice  concentrates, oats, potatoes, raw milk, rice, seasonings, sucralose, sugar , vegetable and essential oils, and wheat. We
also use water in the manufacturing of our products. Our key packaging materials include plastic resins, including polyethylene
terephthalate (PET) and polypropylene resins used for plastic beverage bottles and film packaging used for convenient foods,
aluminum, glass, closures, cardboard and paperboard cartons. In addition, we continue to integrate recyclability into our product
development process and support the increased use of recycled content, including recycled PET, in our packaging. Fuel,
electricity and natural gas are also important commodities for our businesses due to their use in our and our business partners’
facilities and the vehicles delivering our products. We employ specialists to secure adequate supplies of many of these items and
have not experience d any significant continuous shortages that would prevent us from meeting our requirements. Many of these
ingredients, raw materials and commod ities are purchased in the open market. The prices we pay for such items are subject to
fluctuation, and we manage this risk through the use of fixed-price contracts and purchase orders, pricing agreements and
derivative instrumen ts, including swaps and futures. In addition, risk to our supply of certain raw materials is mitigated through
purchases from multiple geographies and suppliers. When prices increase, we may or may not pass on such increases to our
customers. In addition, we continue to make investments to improve the sustainability and resources of our agricultural supply
chain, including the development of our initiative to advance sustainable farming practices by our suppliers and expanding it
further globally . During 2022, we continued to experience increased commodi ty, packaging and other input costs and, in some
instances, supply constraints related to the deadly conflict in Ukraine, the novel coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic, the
inflationary cost environment, adverse weather conditions, supply chain disruptions and labor shortages, which has continued
into fiscal  2023. See Note 9 to our consolidated financial statements for further information on how we manage our exposure to
commodity prices.
We also maintain voluntary supply chain finance agreements with several participating global financial institutions, pursuant to
which our suppliers, at their sole discretion, may elect to sell their accounts receivable with PepsiCo to such global financial
institutions. These agreements did not have a material

impact on our busin ess or financial results. See “Our Financial Results – Our Liquidity and Capital Resources” in “Item 7.
Management’ s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations” for further information.

title: Seasonality
heading: Seasonality
start_phrase: Our businesses are affected by seasona l variations.
summary:
- Extensive overview of brands and intellectual property: large global trademark portfolio across beverages and convenient foods; emphasis on proper trademark use, broad licensing for bottlers, joint ventures, and retail merchandise; ownership/licensing of patents covering products, packaging, processes, and equipment.
- Key brand and partnership moves: distribution of Celsius energy drinks and select Keurig Dr Pepper brands (e.g., Dr Pepper in certain markets, Crush, Schweppes); joint ventures with rights to brands such as Lipton, Sabra, and Starbucks; 2022 sale of Tropicana, Naked and other juice brands to PAI Partners with PepsiCo retaining a 39% noncontrolling interest in TBG and serving as exclusive U.S. distributor for TBG’s chilled DSD in small-format and foodservice; launch of Hard MTN Dew via trademark license to Boston Beer Company with PepsiCo as distributor.
- Seasonality: beverage and snack sales peak in Q3 and are lowest in Q1; overall seasonality not material to consolidated financial results.
- Customer base and routes to market: diverse set of customers including wholesalers, foodservice, mass and dollar retailers, club, convenience, drug, e-commerce, and independent bottlers; exclusive territorial bottling contracts with rights to charge for concentrate/finished goods and Aquafina royalties; defined manufacturing standards and geographic distribution rights.
- Trade and marketing investments: detailed programs for distributors/retailers (volume rebates, placement fees, promotions, displays) and annual bottler funding (consumer incentives, advertising/media support, new product support, vending/cooler placement).
- Retail landscape dynamics: increased retailer consolidation, growth of e-commerce and direct-to-consumer models, omnichannel integration, and international expansion of hard discounters heighten the importance of major customers.
- Customer concentration: Walmart (including Sam’s Club) represented ~14% of 2022 consolidated net revenue; loss of Walmart would materially adversely affect FLNA, QFNA, and PBNA.
- Competitive environment: intense competition from global, regional, local, private label, and micro-brand players; primary beverage competitor is The Coca-Cola Company; other notable competitors include Campbell, Conagra, Hormel, Kellogg, Keurig Dr Pepper, Kraft Heinz, Link Snacks, Mondelēz, Monster, Nestlé, Red Bull, and Utz.
- Market position: strong leadership in many snack categories; in 2022 U.S. liquid refreshment beverages, PepsiCo had ~20% retail share vs. Coca-Cola’s ~21%; Coca-Cola holds CSD share advantages in many markets outside the U.S.
text:
Seasonality
Our businesses are affected by seasona l variations. Our beverage and convenient food sales are generally highest in the third
quarter due to seasonal and holiday-related patterns and generally lowest in the first quarter . However , taken as a whole,
seasonality has not had a material impact on our consolidated financial results.

title: Our Customers
heading: Our Customers
start_phrase: Our custom ers inclu de wholesale and other distributors, foodservice customers, grocery stores, drug stores, convenience stores, discount/dollar stores, mass merchandisers, membership stores, hard discounters, e-commerce retailers and authorized independent bottlers , among others.
summary:
- Customer base spans wholesale and other distributors, foodservice, grocery, drug and convenience stores, discount/dollar and mass merchandisers, membership clubs, hard discounters, e-commerce retailers, and authorized independent bottlers.
- Independent bottlers typically receive exclusive territorial rights to manufacture and/or distribute certain trademarked beverages; the company sells them concentrate/finished goods, charges Aquafina royalties, and prescribes manufacturing standards.
- The company funds trade and consumer programs: for distributors/retailers via volume rebates, placement fees, promotions and displays; for bottlers via annually negotiated “bottler funding” supporting consumer incentives, advertising/media, new product launches (including point-of-purchase and placement fees), and vending/cooler equipment deployment; program mix changes annually.
- Retail landscape shifts—retailer consolidation, growth of e-commerce and mobile commerce (including subscriptions and DTC), omnichannel integration, expansion of hard discounters, and macroeconomic conditions—heighten reliance on major customers.
- Walmart (including Sam’s Club) accounted for ~14% of 2022 consolidated net revenue across divisions (including concentrate sold to bottlers for Walmart-bound finished goods); losing Walmart would materially adversely affect FLNA, QFNA, and PBNA.
- Competitive environment is intense across beverages and convenient foods, with competition from global, regional, local, private-label, and e-commerce-driven microbrands; primary beverage competitor is The Coca-Cola Company.

Our Customers
Our custom ers inclu de wholesale and other distributors, foodservice customers, grocery stores, drug stores, convenience stores,

our trademarks for specified geographic areas.
We rely on and provide financial incentives to our customers to assist in the distribution and promotion of our products to the
consumer . For our independent distributors and retailers, these incentives include volume-based rebates, product placement fees,
promotions and displays. For our independent bottlers, these incentives are referred to as bottler funding and are negotiated
annually with each bottler to support a variety of trade and consumer programs, such as consumer incentives, advertising support,
new product support, and vending and cooler equipment placement. Consumer incentives include pricing discounts and
promotions, and other promotional offers. Advertising support is directed at advertising programs and supporting independent
bottler media. New product support includes targeted consumer and retailer incentives and direct marketplace support, such as
point-of-purchase materials, product placement fees, media and advertising. Vending and cooler equipment placement programs
support the acquisition and placement  of vending machines and cooler equipment. The nature and type of programs vary
annually .
Changes to the retail landscape, includi ng increased consolidation of retail ownership, the continued growth of sales through e-
commerce websites  and mobile comme rce applications, including through subscription services and other direct-to-consumer
businesses, the integration of physical and digital operations among retailers, as well as the international expansion of hard
discounters, and the current economic environment continue to increase the importance of major customers. In 2022, sales to
Walmart Inc. (Walmart) and its affiliates, including Sam’ s Club (Sam’ s), represented approximately 14% of our consolidated net
revenue, with sales reported across all of our divisions, including concentrate sales to our independent bottlers, which were used
in finished  goods sold by them to Walmart. The loss of this customer would have a material adverse effect on our FLNA, QFNA
and PBNA divisions.

text:
Regulatory Matters
The conduct of our businesses, including the production, storage, distribution, sale, display , advertising, marketing, labeling,
content, quality , safety, transportation, packaging, disposal, recycling and use of our products, as well as our employment and
occupational health and safety practices and protection of personal information, are subject to various laws and regulations
administered by federal, state and local governmental agencies in the United States, as well as to laws and regulations
administered by government entities and agencies in the more than 200 other countries and territories in which our products are
made, manufactured , distributed or sold. It is our policy to abide by the laws and regulations around the world that apply to our
businesses.
The U.S. laws and regulations that we are subject to include, but are not limited to: the Federal Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act and
various state laws governing food safety; the Food Safety Modernization Act; the Occupational Safety and Health Act and
various state laws and regulations governing workplace health
8Table of Contents
and safety; various federal, state and local environmental protection laws, as discussed below; the Federal Motor Carrier Safety
Act; the Federal Trade Commission Act; the Lanham Act; various federal and state laws and regulations governing competition
and trade practices, including the Robi nson-Patman Act and the Clayton Act; various federal and state laws and regulations
governing our employment practices, including those related to equal employm ent opportunity , such as the Equal Employment
Opportunity Act and the National Labor Relations Act and those related to overtime compensation, such as the Fair Labor
Standards Act; various state and federal laws pertaining to sale and distribution  of alcohol beverages; data privacy and personal
data protection laws and regulations, including the California Consumer Privacy Act of 2018 (as modified by the California
Privacy Rights Act); customs and foreign trade laws and regulations, including laws regarding the import or export of our
products or ingredients used in our products and tariffs; laws regulating the sale of certain of our products in schools; laws
regulating the ingredients or substances contained in, or attributes of, our products; laws regulating our supply chain, including
the 2010 California Transparency in Supply Chains Act and laws relating to the payment of taxes. We are also required to comply
with the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act and the Trade Sanctions Reform and Export Enhancement Act. We are also subject to
various state and local statutes and regulations, including state consumer protection laws such as Proposition 65 in California,
which requires that a specific warning appear on any product that contains a substance listed by the State of California as having
been found to cause cancer or birth defects, unless the amount of such substance in the product is below a safe harbor level.
We are subject to numerous similar and other laws and regulations outside the United States, including but not limited to laws
and regulations governing food safety , international trade and tariffs, supply chains, including the U.K. Modern Slavery Act,
occupational health  and safety , competition, anti-corruption and data privacy , including the European Union General Data
Protection Regulatio n. In many jurisdictions, compliance with competition laws is of special importance to us due to our
competitive position in those jurisdictions, as is compliance with anti-corruptio n laws, including the U.K. Bribery Act. We rely
on legal and operational compliance programs, as well as in-house and outside counsel and other experts, to guide our businesses
in complying with the laws and regulations around the world that apply to our businesses.
In addition , certain jurisdictions have either imposed, or are considering imposing, new or increased taxes on the manufacture,
distribution or sale of our products, ingredients or substances contained in, or attributes of, our products or commodities used in
the production of our products. These  taxes vary in scope and form: some apply to all beverages, including non-caloric
beverages, while others apply only to beverages with a caloric sweetener (e.g.,  sugar). Similarly , some measures apply a single
tax rate per ounce/l iter on beverages containing over a certain level of added sugar (or other sweetener) while others apply a
graduated tax rate depending upon the amount of added sugar (or other sweeten er) in the beverage and some apply a flat tax rate
on beverages containing a particular substance or ingredient, regardless of the level of such substance or ingredient.
In addition, certain jurisdictions have either imposed, or are considering imposing, product labeling or warning requirements or
other limitations on the marketing or sale of certain of our products as a result of ingredients or substances contained in such
products or the audience to whom products are marketed. These types of provisions have required that we highlight perceived
concerns about a product, warn consum ers to avoid consumption of certain ingredients or substances present in our products,
restrict the age of consumers to whom products are marketed or sold or limit the location in which our products may be available.
It is possible that similar or more restrictive requirements may be proposed or enacted in the future.
In addition, certain jurisdictions have either imposed or are considering imposing regulations designed to increase recycling rates,
encourage waste reduction or to restrict the sale of products utilizing certain packaging. These regulations vary in scope and form
from deposit return systems designed to incentivize
9Table of Contents
the return of beverage containers, to extended producer responsibility policies and even restrictions or bans on the use of certain
types of packaging, including single-us e plastics and packaging containing per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS). It is
possible that similar or more restrictive requirements may be proposed or enacted in the future.
We are also subject to national and local environmental laws in the United States and in foreign countries in which we do
business, including laws related to water consumption and treatment, wastewater dischar ge and air emissions. In the United
States, we are subje ct to the Clean Air Act, the Clean Water Act, the Compre hensive Environmental Response, Compensation
and Liability Act, the Resource Conserv ation and Recovery Act and other federal, state and local laws and regulations regarding
handling, storage, release and disposal of wastes generated onsite and sent to third-party owned and operated offsite licensed
facilities. Our operations outside the United States are subject to similar laws and regulations. In addition, continuing concern
over environmental , social and govern ance matters, including climate change, is expected to continue to result in new or
increased legal and regulatory requirem ents (in or outside of the United States) to reduce emissions to mitigate the potential
effects of greenhous e gases, to limit or impose additional costs on commercial water use due to local water scarcity concerns or
to expand mandatory reporting of certain environmental, social and governance  metrics. Our policy is to abide by all applicable
environmental laws and regulations, and we have internal programs in place with respect to our global environmental
compliance. We have made, and plan to continue making, necessary expenditures for compliance with applicable environmental
laws and regulation s and to achieve our sustainability goals. While these expenditures have not had a material impact on our
business, financial condition or results of operations to date, changes in environmental compliance requirements, and
expenditures necessary to comply with such requirements or to achieve our sustainability goals, could adversely affect our
financial performance. In addition, we and our subsidiaries are subject to environmental remediation obligations arising in the
normal course of business, as well as remediation and related indemnification obligations in connection with certain historical
activities and contractual obligations, including those of businesses or properties acquired by us or our subsidiaries. While these
environmental remediation and indemni fication obligations cannot be predicted with certainty , such obligations have not had, and
are not expected to have, a material impact on our capital expenditures, earnings or competitive position.
In addition to the discussion in this section, see also “Item 1A. Risk Factors.”

text:
Human Capital
PepsiCo believes that human capital management, including attracting, developing and retaining a high quality workforce, is
critical to our long-term success. Our Board of Directors (Board) and its Committees provide oversight on a broad range of
human capital management topics, including corporate culture, diversity , equity and inclusion, pay equity , health and safety ,
training and development and compensation and benefits.
We emplo yed appro ximately 315,000 people worldwide as of December 31, 2022, including approximately 132,000 people
within the United States. We are party to numerous collective bargaining agreements and believe that relations with our
employees are generally good.
Protecting the safety , health, and well-b eing of our associates around the world is PepsiCo’ s top priority . We strive to achieve an
injury-free work environment. We also continue to invest in emer ging technologies to protect our employees from injuries,
including leveraging fleet telematics and distracted driving technology , resulting in reductions in road traffic incidents, and
deploying ergonomic and machine safety risk reduction solutions. In addition , throughout the COVID-19 pandemic, we have
remained focused on the health and safety of our associates, especially our frontline associates who continue to make, move and
sell our products during this critical time, including by continuing to imple ment various safety protocols in our facilities,
providing personal protective equipment and enabling testing. W e are
10Table of Contents
also focused on the safety of our associates in Ukraine and have provided humanitarian aid, goods and services to support our
people and communities facing the ongoing deadly conflict.
We believ e that our culture of diversity , equity and inclusion is a competitive advantage that fuels innovation, enhances our
ability to attract and retain talent and strengthens our reputation. We continual ly strive to improve the attraction, retention, and
advancement of diverse associates to ensure we sustain a high-caliber pipeline of talent that also represents the communities we
serve. As of December 31, 2022, our global workforce was approximately 27% female, while management roles were
approximately 44% female. As of December 31, 2022, approximately 48% of our U.S. workforce was comprised of
racially/ethnically diverse individuals, of which approximately 33% of our U.S. associates in managerial roles were
racially/ethnically diverse individuals. The Board has overseen appointments of current direct reports of our Chief Executive
Officer, who include 7 executives globally who are racially/ethnically diverse and/or female.
We are also committed to the continued growth and development of our associates. PepsiCo supports and develops its associates
through a variety of global training and development programs that build and strengthen employees' leadership and professional
skills, including career development plans, mentoring programs and in-house learning opportunities, such as PEP U Degreed, our
internal global online learning resource. In 2022, PepsiCo employees completed over 1 million hours of training.

start_phrase: The deadly conflict in Ukraine has continued to result in worldwide geopolitical and macroeconomic uncertainty and certain of our opera tions in Ukraine remain suspended.
summary:
- Describes business risks, emphasizing the ongoing impacts of the Ukraine conflict: suspended operations in Ukraine; heightened geopolitical and macroeconomic uncertainty; commodity price volatility; supply chain and logistics disruptions; increased cyber/IT risks; employee safety concerns; labor shortages; Russian ruble volatility; constrained access to credit and banking services (including working capital); higher transportation, energy, packaging and raw material costs; environmental, health and safety challenges at facilities; additional sanctions/export controls and fund transfer restrictions; potential asset losses or impairments; and adverse effects on sustainability goals and global demand.

- Explains risk of reduced future demand tied to the company’s ability to innovate and respond to evolving consumer preferences and channels (e-commerce and online-to-offline), pricing and product quality expectations, environmental concerns about packaging (e.g., single-use plastics), perceptions of nutrition and ingredient origin (including from third-party studies), and shifts due to pandemics/epidemics. Highlights the influence of brand image, marketing effectiveness, digital engagement and social media, and responses to political/social issues. Notes that misreading trends or underinvesting (including in data analytics) can lead to lower demand, inventory write-offs, and weakened competitive/financial position. Warns that natural disasters, pandemics, and other uncontrollable events can disrupt supply, reduce product availability, and dampen demand if crisis management is ineffective.

- Identifies reputation and brand image risk: sales depend on maintaining a positive global reputation, which can be damaged by failures by the company or its partners to uphold ethical standards and ESG practices, including compliance with human rights and child labor laws and commitments to diversity, equity and inclusion.
text:
Risks associated with the deadly conflict in Ukraine
The deadly conflict in Ukraine has continued to result in worldwide geopolitical and macroeconomic uncertainty and certain of
our opera tions in Ukraine remain suspended. The conflict has resulted and could continue to result in volatile commodity
markets, supply chain disruptions, increased risk of cyber incidents or other disruptions to our information systems, reputational
risk, heigh tened risks to employee safety, business disruptions (including labor shortages), significant volatility of the Russian
ruble, limitations on access to credit markets and other corporate banking services, including working capital facilities, reduced
availability and increased costs for transportation, energy, packaging and raw materials and other input costs, environmental,
health and safety risks related to securing and maintaining facilities, additional sanctions, export controls and other legislation or
regulations (including restrictions on the transfer of funds to and from Russia). The ongoing conflict could result in the temporary
or permanent loss of assets or result in additional impairment charges. We canno t predict how and the extent to which the conflict
will contin ue to affect our employees, operations, customers, consumers or business partners or our ability to achieve certain of
our sustainability goals. The conflict has adversely affected and could continue to adversely affect demand for our products and
our global business.

title: Reduction in future demand for our products would adversely affect our business.
heading: Reduction in future demand for our products would adversely af fect our business.
start_phrase: Demand for our products depends in part on our ability to innovate and anticipate and effectively respond to shifts in consumer trends and preferenc es, including the types of products our consumers want and how they browse for, purchase and consume them.
summary: The partial document outlines key business risks. It highlights extensive impacts from the conflict in Ukraine, including suspended operations, geopolitical and macroeconomic uncertainty, supply chain and cyber disruptions, employee safety risks, labor shortages, ruble volatility, restricted access to credit and banking services, rising costs for transportation, energy, packaging and raw materials, evolving sanctions/export controls, potential asset losses or impairments, and possible setbacks to sustainability goals and product demand. It details risks of reduced future demand driven by failure to innovate or anticipate shifting consumer preferences across channels (including e-commerce), concerns about packaging and environmental impact (e.g., plastics), perceptions of nutrition/ingredient origin influenced by third-party studies, pricing and product quality, pandemic-driven demand shifts, brand image and marketing effectiveness, digital engagement, and reactions to social/political issues that may spur boycotts; it also notes the potential for inventory write-offs and operational disruptions from natural disasters and disease outbreaks if crisis management is ineffective. Finally, it underscores reputational risk, where failures by the company or its partners to uphold strong ethical, business, and ESG standards—covering areas like human rights, child labor, diversity, and equity—can damage brand image and adversely affect the business.
text:
Demand for our products depends in part on our ability to innovate and anticipate and effectively respond to shifts in consumer
trends and preferenc es, including the types of products our consumers want and how they browse for, purchase and consume
them. Consumer preferences continuously evolve due to a variety of factors,  including: changes in consumer demographics,
consumption pattern s and channel prefe rences (including continued increases in the e-commerce and online-to-of fline channels);
pricing; product quality; concerns or perceptions regarding packaging and its environmental impact (such as single-use and other
plastic packaging); and concerns or perceptions regarding the nutrition profile and health effects of, or location of origin of,
ingredients or substances in our products or packaging, including due to the results of third-party studies (whether or not
scientifically valid).  Concerns with any of the foregoing could lead consumers to reduce or publicly boycott the purchase or
consumption of our products. Pandemics, epidemics or other disease outbreaks, such as COVID-19, have also impacted and
could continue to impact consumer preferences and demand for our products. Consumer preferences are also influenced by
perception of our brand image or the brand images of our products, the success of our advertising and marketing campaigns, our
ability to engage with our consumers in the manner they prefer , including through the use of digital media or assets, and the
perception of our use, the use of social media and our response to political and social issues or catastrophic events. These and
other facto rs have reduced in the past and could continue to reduce consumers’  willingness to purchase certain of our products.
Any inabi lity on our part to anticipate or react to changes in consumer preferences and trends, or make the right strategic
investments to do so, including investments in data analytics to understand consumer trends, can lead to reduced demand for our
products, lead to inventory write-of fs or erode our competitive and financial position, thereby adversely affecting our business. In
addition, our business operations, including our supply chain, are subject to disruption by natural disasters, pandemics, epidemics
or other events beyo nd our control that could negatively impact product availab ility and decrease demand for our products if our
crisis management plans do not ef fectively mitigate these issues.

title: Damage to our reputation or brand image can adversely affect our business.
heading: Damage to our reputation or brand image can adversely af fect our business.
start_phrase: Maintaining a positive reputation globally is critical to selling our products.
summary:
- Focus on Business Risks, emphasizing how external events and internal execution can adversely affect operations, demand, and financial performance.
- Ukraine conflict risks: suspended operations in parts of Ukraine; heightened geopolitical and macroeconomic uncertainty; volatile commodity markets; supply chain disruptions; increased cyber risk; employee safety concerns; business disruptions (including labor shortages); ruble volatility; restricted access to credit and banking services (e.g., working capital); higher transportation, energy, packaging, and raw material costs; environmental, health and safety risks in maintaining facilities; sanctions and export controls (including fund transfer restrictions); potential asset loss or impairments; negative impacts on demand and sustainability goals.
- Demand volatility: need to anticipate and respond to shifting consumer preferences across channels (e-commerce, online-to-offline), pricing, product quality, packaging sustainability (e.g., plastics), nutrition/health and ingredient-origin concerns (including from third-party studies), and pandemic-driven behavior changes; dependence on brand image, effective advertising/marketing, digital engagement and social media; risks from public responses to political/social issues or catastrophic events; failure to invest in data analytics or make the right strategic choices can reduce demand, cause inventory write-offs, and erode competitiveness; natural disasters/pandemics can disrupt supply and depress demand if crisis plans are ineffective.
- Reputation/brand image: vulnerability to perceived or actual failures in ethics and ESG (human rights, child labor, DEI, workplace conditions, employee health/safety); not meeting ESG goals (nutrition profile, packaging, water, environmental impact); handling of health concerns (including alcoholic beverages distributed); R&D outcomes; product quality/safety issues and recalls; compliance with laws and regulations; perceptions of advertising, sponsorships, social media use, and responses to social/political events; inability to counter negative commentary can reduce demand.
- Product quality and safety: recalls due to mislabeling, misbranding, spoilage, undeclared allergens, adulteration, or contamination (including at joint ventures); costs from recalls, destroyed inventory, lost sales, production/delivery disruptions, fines/judgments, and reputational harm; expanding into new categories (e.g., alcohol) increases exposure; inadequate oversight may trigger recalls, litigation, investigations, and civil/criminal liability; category-wide loss of confidence can harm the business even if unrelated to its products.
- Competitive dynamics: intense competition from global peers, regional/local players, private label/economy brands, and direct-to-consumer micro brands; Coca-Cola cited as primary beverage competitor in many markets; competition based on brand strength, taste, price/value, quality, variety/innovation, distribution, marketing/promotion, packaging, convenience, service, and responsiveness to trends; risks if unable to promote existing products, launch/market new ones, adopt technologies (AI, data analytics), enhance digital marketing, or counter competitor spending, supply disruptions, and commodity-driven pricing pressure, potentially weakening competitive and financial position.
text:
Maintaining a positive reputation globally is critical to selling our products. Our reputation or brand image has in the past been,
and could in the future be, adversely impacted by a variety of factors, including: any failure by us or our business partners to
maintain high ethical, business and environmental, social and governance practices, including with respect to human rights, child
labor laws, diversity , equity and

environmental, social and governance goals, including with respect to the nutrition profile of our products, diversity , equity and
inclusion initiatives,  packaging, water use and our impact on the environment; any failure to address health or other concerns

title: Product recalls or other issues or concerns with respect to product quality and safety can adversely affect our business.
heading: Product recalls or other issues or concerns with respect to product quality and safety can adversely af fect our business.
start_phrase: We have and could in the future recall products due to product quality or safety issues, including actual or alleged mislabeling, misbranding, spoilage, undeclared allergens, adulteration or contamination.
summary:
- Reputational and brand risks from perceived or actual shortcomings in ESG commitments (nutrition profile, diversity, equity and inclusion, packaging, water use, environmental impact), handling of health concerns about products/ingredients (including obesity), R&D outcomes, and public responses to advertising, sponsorships, social media, and social/political events; inability to counter negative commentary can reduce demand.

- Product quality and safety risks, including recalls due to mislabeling, misbranding, spoilage, undeclared allergens, adulteration or contamination—also affecting joint ventures and new categories like alcoholic beverage distribution. Consequences include inventory loss, sales disruption, increased costs, fines/judgments, litigation, investigations, potential civil/criminal liability, production/delivery disruptions, reputational damage, and broader loss of consumer confidence; underscores need for strong quality oversight.

- Competitive pressures from global players (notably The Coca‑Cola Company), regional/local brands, private label/economy brands, and smaller direct-to-consumer micro brands. Competition centers on brand loyalty, taste, price/value, quality, variety, innovation, distribution, advertising/marketing/promotions, packaging, convenience, service, and responsiveness to consumer trends.

- Operational and strategic requirements to remain competitive: effectively promote existing products and launch new ones; adopt technologies (including AI and data analytics) to generate insights and improve efficiency; strengthen digital marketing; and respond to supply disruptions and pricing pressure (including commodity inflation). Failure in these areas can adversely affect the business.
text:
Product recalls or other issues or concerns with respect to product quality and safety can adversely af fect our business.
We have and could in the future recall products due to product quality or safety issues, including actual or alleged mislabeling,
misbranding, spoilage, undeclared allergens, adulteration or contamination. Joint ventures in which we have an interest have also
recalled, and could in the future recall, products for the same or other reasons. Product recalls have in the past and could in the
future adversely affect our business by resulting in losses due to their cost, the destruction of product inventory or lost sales due
to any unavailability  of the product for a period of time. In addition, product quality or safety issues, whether as a result of failure
to comply with food safety laws or otherwise, have in the past and could in the future also reduce consumer confidence and
demand for our products, cause production and delivery disruptions, and result in increased costs (including payment of fines
and/or judgments) and damage our reput ation (or the reputation of joint ventures in which we have an interest), particularly as we
or our joint venture s continue to expand into new categories, such as the distribution of alcoholic beverages, all of which can
adversely affect our business. Failure to maintain adequate oversight over product quality or safety can result in product recalls,
litigation, government investigations or inquiries or civil or criminal proceedings, all of which may result in fines, penalties,
damages or criminal liability . Our busin ess can also be adversely affected if consumers lose confidence in product quality , safety
and integrity generally , even if such loss of confidence is unrelated to products in our portfolio.

title: Any inability to compete effectively can adversely affect our business.
heading: Any inability to compete ef fectively can adversely af fect our business.
start_phrase: Our produ cts compete against products of international beverage and convenient food companies that, like us, operate in multiple geographies, as well as regional, local and private label and economy brand manufacturers and other competitors, including smaller companies developing and selling micro brands directly to consumers through e-commerce platforms or through retailers focused on locally sourced products.
summary:
- Reputation and ESG risks: Potential harm from failing to meet environmental, social and governance goals (nutrition profile, DEI initiatives, packaging, water use, environmental impact), negative consumer perceptions of advertising, sponsorships, marketing, and responses to political/social events, and social media backlash—any of which can reduce demand.
- Product quality and safety: Risks of recalls due to mislabeling, allergens, contamination, spoilage or adulteration, including in joint ventures and new categories like alcoholic beverages; consequences include lost sales, destroyed inventory, production/distribution disruptions, fines, litigation, investigations, and lasting brand damage—even broader loss of confidence in product safety across the market.
- Competitive dynamics: Intense competition from global players (with The Coca-Cola Company as primary beverage rival), regional/local/private label brands, and direct-to-consumer micro brands; competition on brand, taste, price, quality, innovation, distribution, marketing, packaging, convenience, and responsiveness to trends; need to adopt technologies (AI, data analytics), strengthen digital marketing, and address supply disruptions and commodity inflation to protect sales and share.
- Talent and workforce: Dependence on attracting, developing, and retaining a diverse, highly skilled workforce amid labor shortages, wage inflation, higher turnover, remote-work shifts, and succession risks (including CEO); critical needs in e-commerce, digital marketing, and data analytics; failure can raise costs, erode institutional knowledge and competitive advantage, and harm reputation and results.
- Water scarcity: Vulnerability due to water’s role in manufacturing and raw materials; climate change and stakeholder/regulatory pressures may trigger supply chain disruptions, higher compliance and capital costs (efficiency investments), increased water prices, operational interruptions/relocations, missed water-use goals, and reputational harm.
- Evolving retail landscape: Growth of e-commerce and hard discounters requiring new partnerships and digital capabilities while maintaining traditional retail relationships; risks if these channels take share from traditional retailers or if direct-to-consumer efforts are not profitable; increasing retailer consolidation in North America, Europe, and Latin America boosts buyer power and pressures pricing, while straining smaller customers’ viability and orders.
text:
Our produ cts compete against products of international beverage and convenient food companies that, like us, operate in multiple
geographies, as well as regional, local and private label and economy brand manufacturers and other competitors, including
smaller companies developing and selling micro brands directly to consumers through e-commerce platforms or through retailers
focused on locally sourced products. In many countries in which our products are sold, including the United States, The Coca-
Cola Company is our primary beverage competitor . Our products compete primarily on the basis of brand recognition and loyalty ,
taste, price , value, quality , product varie ty, innovation, distribution, advertising, marketing and promotional activity , packaging,
convenience, service and the ability to anticipate and effectively respond to consumer preferences and trends. Our business can
be adverse ly affected if we are unable to effectively promote or develop our existing products or introduce and effectively market
new products, if we are unable to effectively adopt new technologies, including artificial intelligence and data analytics to
develop new commercial insights and improve operating efficiencies, if we are unable to continuously strengthen and evolve our
capabilities in digital marketing, if our competitors spend more aggressively than we do or if we are otherwise unable to
effectively respond to supply disruptions, pricing pressure (including as a result of commodity inflation) or otherwise compete
effectively , and we may be

title: Failure to attract, develop and maintain a highly skilled and diverse workforce or effectively manage changes in our workforce can have an adverse effect on our business.
heading:
Failure to attract, develop and maintain a highly skilled and diverse workforce or effectively manage changes in our
workforce can have an adverse ef fect on our business.
start_phrase: Our busin ess requires that we attract, develop and maintain a highly skilled and diverse workforce.
summary:
- Ongoing pressure to maintain or grow sales and category share, potentially requiring increased capital, marketing, and other expenditures.
- Talent and workforce risks: intense competition for skilled, diverse employees; wage inflation, labor shortages, higher turnover, remote-work shifts; succession planning (including CEO); need for e-commerce, digital marketing, and data analytics capabilities; potential loss of institutional knowledge, higher costs, and reputational harm if diversity goals aren’t met.
- Water scarcity risks: heavy reliance on water in operations and supply chain; climate change and stakeholder pressure driving conservation; potential for supply disruptions, higher compliance and capital costs, increased production costs, facility interruptions or relocations, failure to meet water goals, regulatory challenges, and reputational damage.
- Retail landscape shifts: growth of e-commerce and hard discounters; necessity to strengthen relationships across channels and build digital tools for retail partners; challenges in profitably expanding direct-to-consumer e-commerce; industry consolidation increasing retailer purchasing power in North America, Europe, and Latin America, which can pressure margins, weaken competitiveness, strain smaller customers, and lead to reduced or canceled orders; heightened dependence on key customers.
text:
Failure to attract, develop and maintain a highly skilled and diverse workforce or effectively manage changes in our
workforce can have an adverse ef fect on our business.
Our busin ess requires that we attract, develop and maintain a highly skilled and diverse workforce. Our employees are highly
sought after by our competitors and other companies and our continued ability to compete effectively depends on our ability to
attract, retain, develop and motivate highly skilled personnel for all areas of our organization. Our ability to do so has been and
may conti nue to be impacted by challenges in the labor market, which has experienced and may continue to experience wage
inflation, labor shortages, increased employee turnover , changes in availability of our workforce and a shift toward remote work.
Any unpla nned turnover , sustained labor shortage or unsuccessful implementation of our succession plans to backfill current
leadership positions, including the Chief Executive Officer, or failure to attract, develop and maintain a highly skilled and diverse
workforce, including with key capabilities such as e-commerce and digital marketing and data analytic skills, can deplete our
institutional knowledge base, erode our competitive advantage or result in increased costs due to increased competition for
employees, higher employee turnover or increased employee benefit costs. In addition, failure to attract, retain and develop
associates from underrepresented communities can damage our business results and our reputation. Any of the foregoing can
adversely af fect our business.

title: Water scarcity can adversely affect our business.
heading: Water scarcity can adversely af fect our business.
start_phrase: We and our business partners use water in the manufacturing of our products.
summary:
- Highlights risk of stagnating or declining sales and market share, potentially requiring increased capital, marketing, or other expenditures.
- Emphasizes workforce risks: intense competition for talent; wage inflation, labor shortages, higher turnover, and remote-work shifts; importance of succession planning (including CEO); and need for skills in e-commerce, digital marketing, and data analytics. Notes potential impacts such as loss of institutional knowledge, higher costs, reduced competitiveness, and reputational harm, including from failing to attract and develop diverse talent.
- Details water scarcity risks: dependence on water for manufacturing and raw materials; climate-change-driven scarcity; stakeholder pressures to conserve/replenish water; possible supply chain disruptions, higher compliance and capital costs (e.g., water-efficiency technologies), increased production costs, operational interruptions/relocations, failure to meet water goals, and reputational damage.
- Describes retail landscape shifts: growth of e-commerce channels and hard discounters; necessity of strong partnerships with both emerging and traditional retailers; need to build superior digital tools for retail partners and expand profitable direct-to-consumer capabilities. Warns of retail consolidation in North America, Europe, and Latin America increasing buyer power, pressuring competitiveness and margins, and straining smaller customers, which can lead to payment issues or reduced/canceled orders.
text:
We and our business  partners use water in the manufacturing of our products. Water is also essential to the production of the raw
materials needed in our manufacturing process. Lack of available water of acceptable quality , actions by governmental and non-
governmental organizations, investors, customers and consumers on water scarcity and increasing pressure to conserve and
replenish water in areas of scarcity and stress, including due to the effects of climate change, can lead to: supply chain disruption;
adverse effects on our operations or the operations of our business partners; higher compliance costs; increased capital
expenditures (including investments in the development of technologies to enhance water efficiency and reduce consumption);
higher production costs, including less favorable pricing for water; the interruption or cessation of operations at, or relocation of,
our facilities or the facilities of our business partners; failure to achieve our goals relating to water use; perception of our failure
to act responsibly with respect to water use or to effectively respond to legal or regulatory requirements concerning water
scarcity; or damage to our reputation, any of which can adversely af fect our business.

title: Changes in the retail landscape or in sales to any key customer can adversely affect our business.
heading: Changes in the retail landscape or in sales to any key customer can adversely af fect our business.
start_phrase: The retail landscape continues to evolve, including continued growth in e-commerce channels and hard discounters.
summary:
- Overall risk that failure to grow sales or category share may require increased capital, marketing, or other spending.
- Talent and workforce risks: difficulty attracting, developing, and retaining a highly skilled and diverse workforce amid wage inflation, labor shortages, higher turnover, and shifts to remote work; succession planning challenges (including CEO); need for e-commerce, digital marketing, and data analytics capabilities; potential reputational and performance impacts from insufficient diversity and inclusion.
- Water scarcity risks: heavy reliance on water for manufacturing and raw materials; scarcity/quality issues and stakeholder pressure can drive supply chain disruptions, higher compliance and capital costs (e.g., efficiency technologies), increased production costs, operational interruptions or relocation, inability to meet water goals, and reputational damage.
- Retail landscape changes: continued rise of e-commerce and hard discounters; need to sustain relationships across channels and build better digital tools for retailers; challenges in profitably expanding direct-to-consumer; consolidation increasing retailers’ purchasing power and pressuring margins; smaller customers’ reduced ability to compete or pay; dependence on key customers (e.g., Walmart) with risks from disputes, financial stress, reduced orders, or loss.
- Manufacturing and supply chain disruptions and cost inflation: sourcing from unstable regions; limited/sole-source materials; seasonal shortages; volatility in prices and availability of commodities, fuel, packaging (including recycled PET), transportation, and labor due to supply-demand shifts, capacity constraints, inflation, weather/climate change, natural disasters, disease/pests (e.g., citrus greening), epidemics/pandemics (including COVID-19), labor shortages/strikes (including rail), trade restrictions (tariffs, sanctions, quotas), port congestion, transport constraints, cybersecurity incidents, loss of key sites, political instability, terrorism, and currency movements. Noted higher-than-expected commodity, packaging, and transport costs in 2022; limited ability to raise prices or hedge can reduce volume, revenue, margins, and results.
- Political and social instability: elections, referendums, government shutdowns, and hostilities can alter or create uncertainty around laws and policies (tariffs, sanctions, environmental/climate rules, taxes, benefits, cross-border movement), leading to exchange rate volatility, stock market swings, global economic uncertainty, and weaker demand.
text:
The retail landscape continues to evolve, including continued growth in e-commerce channels and hard discounters. Our business
will be adversely affected if we are unable to maintain and develop successful relationships with e-commerce retailers and hard
discounters, while also maintaining relationships with our key customers operating in traditional retail channels (many of whom
are also focused on increasing their e-commerce sales). Our business can be adversely affected if e-commerce channels and hard
discounters take significant additional market share away from traditional retail ers or we fail to find ways to create increasingly
better digital tools and capabilities for our retail customers to enable them to grow their businesses. In addition, our business can
be adversely affected if we are unable to profitably expand our own direct-to-consumer e-commerce capabilities. The retail
industry is also impacted by increased consolidation of ownership and purchasing power , particularly in North America, Europe
and Latin  America, resulting in large retailers or buying groups with increased purchasing power , impacting our ability to
compete in these areas. Consolidation also adversely impacts our smaller customers’ ability to compete ef fectively , resulting in an
inability on their part to pay for our products or reduced or canceled orders of our products. Further , we must maintain mutually
beneficial relationships with our key
